title: 7 moments you might have missed at the 2026 Italian Grand Prix
excerpt:
Monza delivered another dramatic Sunday, with the Temple of Speed bringing plenty of action throughout the 53-lap Italian Grand Prix.

On track, home race hero Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes took a spectacular victory from 19th on the grid, ahead of team mate George Russell and Max Verstappen of Red Bull, whilst Charles Leclerc’s race came to an early end on Lap 2 after the Ferrari driver crashed at the exit of the Parabolica as he fought McLaren's Oscar Piastri for position, bringing out the red flags.

However, those weren’t the only stories from the Italian weekend – here are some moments you may have missed…

In the name of Michael

Thirty years on from Michael Schumacher’s Ferrari debut, Monza provided the setting for a particularly special tribute to the seven-time World Champion courtesy of another German great.

Ahead of Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix, Sebastian Vettel – who raced for the Scuderia between 2015 and 2020 - returned to the wheel of Schumacher’s Ferrari F2002, taking the iconic car around Monza in front of the Tifosi.

The F2002 remains one of Ferrari’s most successful cars, taking 15 victories across the 2002 and 2003 seasons, but it was the unmistakable sound of its V10 engine that really turned heads around Monza.

“There is still a race to win, for my friend Michael,” Vettel wrote on social media.

Piazza Del Duomo is red – again!

Nothing says Italian Grand Prix weekend more than a Piazza Del Duomo in Milano full of Tifosi in red.

Ferrari fans once again had the chance to show all their love and support to their favourite drivers in an entertaining afternoon with Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton and some special guests.

What better way to celebrate with fans than some modern music and a special DJ, with such an iconic backdrop?

South Korean DJ, Peggy Gou, was the star of the musical entertainment, and Leclerc decided to give it a shot too...but after his attempt at spinning the decks, perhaps it’s better if the two-time Italian GP race winner sticks to driving cars.

And for such a special day, a special guest was needed. And who is more special than a mother?

Hamilton chose to share this moment with his mum as Linda enjoyed a deserved response from the crowd with one of the biggest cheers of the day for her and a true Tifosi welcome to Italy.

The seven-time World Champion said of his mum being in Italy: "And my mum’s here this weekend because she’s never experienced — she’s never actually, I don’t think, been to Monza — but also particularly on a Ferrari weekend. And I wanted her to experience that and, you know, bring any of the lucky dust she can bring."

A smooth operation in Venice

The smooth operator himself, Carlos Sainz, swapped the race suit for a more elegant one to wear on the red carpet of the 83rd Venice International Film Festival.

The Williams driver seems at ease in the glamorous scene of Venice, making a statement appearance for Danny Boyle's new film Ink, wearing Giorgio Armani on the red carpet as he was accompanied by his partner Rebecca Donaldson.

Lightning McQueen turns 20

The Disney-Pixar blockbuster Cars turns 20 this year, and to celebrate this special anniversary, the seven-time Piston Cup champion Lightning McQueen landed in Monza.

While the famous movie car didn’t race in the Italian Grand Prix, the Safety Car marked the 20th anniversary with a special livery. For some of the drivers, it was a dream come true to meet their childhood hero in the paddock. Liam Lawson and Franco Colapinto couldn’t resist getting closer to Lightning McQueen.

A special helmet for a special race

It was a home race weekend for Kimi Antonelli with the Italian driver arriving in Monza as the leader in the drivers’ standings, and he could not miss the chance to wear a special helmet in front of his home crowd.

Antonelli was inspired by Italian MotoGP legend Valentino Rossi for its design, creating a new personalised version of the helmet the Doctor wore at the 2002 Mugello Grand Prix.

It featured the Italian flag, vignettes of Italian daily life (including an espresso cup and a slice of pizza), a sun, the sea, a family and then – at the back – two cartoon figures: one Antonelli, the other Rossi.

Kimi Antonelli becomes a...duck

In what proved to be aa memorable weekend for Antonelli, he also entered the Disney universe for one of the most unique moments of his career.

A cartoon version of himself, Kimi Paperelli, made its debut in a series of stories in Topolino magazine this weekend, all set in the world of Duckburg.

Speaking exclusively to F1.com, Joss Hastings, Senior Vice President of Marketing at Disney Consumer Products, explained why Antonelli was the perfect fit for the collaboration.

“Fuel the Magic is all about bringing Disney storytelling into the world of Formula 1 in unexpected and creative ways. Seeing Kimi become Kimi Paperelli is especially meaningful knowing that he grew up reading Topolino and loving Donald Duck."

When in Italy…

In a typical Italian tradition, Barilla chose to bring the Formula 1 family together for a special dinner: a moment to slow down, enjoy good food and good company before all the racing action.

For one evening, F1's Official Pasta Partner transformed the starting grid into a unique dining room, complete with an F1-inspired menu. Diners were treated to a three-course meal, with each course presented as a different 'lap'.

Few dinner reservations come with a view quite like this.

title: Mekies reflects on Red Bull's 'intense' Italian GP
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies believes Red Bull made a "step in the right direction" during last weekend's Italian Grand Prix, as Max Verstappen claimed another podium.

The Dutchman finished best of the rest in Sunday's 53-lap race behind the Mercedes machines of race winner Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, having battled with the duo and even briefly leading.

Red Bull expected to struggle against Mercedes-powered cars along Monza's straights, with Team Principal Mekies pleased that Verstappen was able to beat the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

"Today was a well-deserved podium for Max and the whole team," he said.

"It was an intense weekend, but the race showed that our pace was fairly strong. Mercedes were a bit too fast for us but we were strong enough to beat Ferrari and McLaren on merit. It was probably our best race pace in a few weeks and a step in the right direction.

"We won't be happy until we have that ultimate speed and we clearly still have some challenges to overcome, which may unlock more performance once we get to the bottom of them."

The result was Verstappen's fifth podium of the season and his third in the last four races as Red Bull continue to find improvement after a slow start under the new-for-2026 regulations.

Team mate Liam Lawson, standing in for the injured Isack Hadjar again, was unable to reach the points.

The New Zealander was due to start from the back after several power unit element changes, but started from the pit lane after further changes to his set up were made in parc ferme – while replacing a damaged front wing in the race ultimately meant he finished in P14.

"Max has been incredible on track today. He made several very spectacular overtakes and defensive manoeuvres and drove an aggressive strategy which led us to the podium," added Mekies.

"Liam showed good pace after a challenging start of the race from the back of the grid following his PU penalties. Contact with Nico [Hulkenberg] meant we had to change his front wing and ultimately killed his chance for points.

"We take the improved pace and many learnings from Monza, and look forward to the very new circuit of Madrid in a few days."

title: When F1 met Cars – Celebrating 20 years of the movie
excerpt:
A familiar voice

Although you’ll be familiar with the sound of Owen Wilson, Paul Newman and Richard Petty – voicing Lightning McQueen, Doc Hudson and The King respectively – several members of racing royalty also feature across the 2006 film.

In the first movie, two former World Champions have their own motorised counterparts. The first is Mario Andretti who competed in both F1 and the IndyCar National Championship, taking title honours in both.

He appears as himself in car form ahead of the 200-lap winner-takes-all tiebreaker race at the end of the movie, and is represented by a 1967 Ford Fairlane. The other legend who has his own presence is seven-time F1 World Champion Michael Schumacher, who appears as a 2005 Ferrari F430 at the end of the movie at Luigi’s Casa Della Tires.

Disney-Pixar also reached out to motorsport’s biggest stars for international dubbing. For Mario Andretti’s character, Fernando Alonso is used for Spanish speakers, and in the German version Mika Hakkinen replaces Andretti’s character altogether.

In the Finnish translation, two-time F1 champ Hakkinen also voices The King, with three-time World Champion Niki Lauda completing a voiceover for the same role in the German version. Giancarlo Fisichella also lends his voice to Boost for the Italian version of the film.

For Cars 2, released in 2011, more of the F1 grid got involved in lending their voices to some special characters. Alonso returned, but this time as his own animated car counterpart who attends the World Grand Prix and hangs out with Lightning McQueen in the Spanish version. Sebastian Vettel voiced race car Sebastian Schnell in the German version of the film; in other regions, the character was called Max Schnell and voiced by actors.

Lewis Hamilton also appears in Cars 2, as a character who carries the same name. He too races in the World Grand Prix, and Hamilton was apparently the only voice actor who was directly involved in the design of his persona.

Jacques Villeneuve also made a cameo as a commentator called David Hobbscap in the French-Canadian and French dubs, with Juan Pablo Montoya narrating the race car Jeff Gorvette in the Latin-American versions of the film.

Finally, in Cars 3, Hamilton, Vettel and Alonso all reprise their voices, with each playing the voice assistant of racing driver Cruz Ramirez in their respective regions.

Love for Lightning McQueen

Plenty of drivers have admitted to growing up on the Cars trilogy, with one big fan being Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson. He’s frequently taking photos next to the anthropomorphic stock car, from Disneyland to his recent trip to the Goodwood Festival of Speed.

During an interview in which he spoke about his love for the movie, Lawson was asked by F1 what his own Cars character would be like.

Lawson said in the 2024 interview. “It would have to look cool; it would have to be a cool-looking car; it couldn’t be a boring looking car. Obviously he’d have to be fast, and he’d have to race. He’d have to be like Lightning [McQueen] and he’d have to be in the Piston Cup – he’d have to win the Piston Cup! Number 30 as well.”

Discussing where his love for the movie originated, he told the media: “It was a movie that was very important to me, especially when I was young obviously. As a kid, it was a movie I watched every other day – genuinely – when I was three. Just at the age I was watching racing, and starting go-karts in the next couple of years. It was just a very big movie for me as a kid. I still watch it a lot.”

title: Vasseur promises Ferrari will bounce back in Madrid
excerpt:
It goes without saying that the Italian Grand Prix weekend is the biggest of the year for Ferrari, and over the decades the Tifosi have grown used to experiencing a rollercoaster of highs and lows.

This year’s race promised much, with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton alongside each other on the second row.

However, they managed to trip over each other at the first chicane before Leclerc had a huge crash at Parabolica on the second lap. He escaped unhurt, but the team was left with a wrecked SF-26, and potentially some lost power unit elements.

After the red flag and restart, Hamilton could manage only P6, not the sort of outcome that anyone in the Maranello camp could be too happy about – especially Team Principal Fred Vasseur.

“Tomorrow morning back at the factory we will prepare Madrid, and we'll come to Madrid with all the energy that we need to do a good result,” he said after Sunday's race. “But it's true that Monza for us, even if I spend the week to say that it's a normal race, it's not, as you can imagine.

“And with all the Tifosi this weekend, we were expecting to give them something else as a big thanks for the support and the enthusiasm that they have. But be sure that we'll come back next week much stronger.”

The first corner clash put a renewed focus on the tricky subject of balancing the interests of Leclerc and Hamilton. The latter made it clear after the flag that he feels his World Championship bid needs more support, and that it’s time for rules of engagement to be applied.

Vasseur didn’t want to comment on the specifics of the first lap – he had not yet talked to both drivers – but he made an interesting point about prioritising a title contender.

“For sure, the outcome of Turn 1 and 2 is not good for the team,” said Vasseur. “Now to see if we have a team order or whatever, I think that the good comparison that I made was that last year Piastri was the leading McLaren at this stage of the season – and if McLaren put everything on Piastri, Max Verstappen would have been champion.

“But for sure, at one stage you have to take a decision. But I think it was too early to take a decision before Monza. Now we have time to discuss with the guys.”

While things went awry in the first couple of laps, with one car out and the other tumbling down the order, Vasseur acknowledged that it would still have been a difficult afternoon. That was evidenced by Hamilton’s struggles while battling other cars.

The team’s upgraded power unit was a useful boost, but straight-line performance was still not where it needed to be.

Hamilton reflects on 'devastating' Italian Grand Prix for Ferrari

“There are a lot of ifs,” he said when asked what a clean race would have brought. “And honestly, I can't predict. I think race pace, we showed yesterday the race pace was probably okay-ish. Main issue was top speed and overtaking.

“It means that it was quite impossible for us to attack or to defend. Or when we are attacking someone, we are draining the battery, and next straight line we are losing the position. And it was more than the pace. I think we were a little bit in a corner with the strategy, honestly. We were just stuck with the top speed.

“I think we did a step, but clearly we knew before the weekend that the fight in the race will be critical. When we were putting a bit more energy in one corner, it was even bigger the gap in the next straightline, and it was quite impossible to manage.

“But honestly, this it's not news, and coming to Monza, we knew that it will be like this. Then the circumstances of the race didn't help for sure.”

In the end it comes down to power unit performance, and despite the latest ADUO upgrade, there is still much work to do.

“I don't want to give details,” said Vasseur. “But when you have a lack of pure power, then you start to play with deployment to try to compensate in one straight line, but if you deploy more somewhere, for sure you will deploy less somewhere else, and then you are going in the wrong spiral to try to play with this when you are fighting.

“Honestly, it's not about deployment. I think deployment it was okay-ish. Even McLaren they were playing a little bit Friday and Saturday morning. At the end, we are missing pure power.”

That won’t be so critical at next weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix, where the team will have an early chance to make amends for the Monza frustration.

“It's very early to think about Madrid, and to have expectations for Madrid. I have to digest the weekend, but for sure the layout of the track is probably fitting a bit more with what we have today, and we can expect a bit more next week. But first, let me let me digest this.”

title: Why McLaren let Norris and Piastri race at Monza
excerpt:
On Saturday evening at Monza, McLaren Team Principal Andrea Stella was adamant that poor execution was the root cause of a disappointing Q3 outcome that saw Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris start in P6 and P8.

After Sunday’s hectic race saw them move up to P4 and P5 – with Norris ahead this time – the Italian acknowledged a much better overall performance, and pretty much the optimum that the team could have expected given the weakness of the MCL40 package on the straights.

It was also a race where Norris and Piastri were allowed to race without intervention, giving fans a second battle to watch in the closing laps along with that between the Mercedes drivers for the lead.

“I think this is a race in which we executed racing better than what we did yesterday,” said Stella.

“Yesterday in Qualifying we should have qualified certainly better than a P6/P8 on the grid. And we reviewed that with the team and with the drivers, and we said to ourselves that today, from an execution point of view, we should have done better and operated higher standards.

“I think overall, we did. We paid a bit of price of the position on the grid... it is not easy to get an overtake completed and move on – like if we see how much it took for Lando to pass [Pierre] Gasly, and then start to close the gap to the cars ahead.

“We see that there's certainly been quite a lot of entertainment today, but to some extent there were also some issues for a quicker car to be able to compete, if you don't start at the front of the grid. Very, very busy [for] everyone, drivers and engineers, with managing the power unit and the battery in a circuit like Monza.”

The battle between Piastri and Norris provided great entertainment, and there was a logical reason behind the team allowing it to run its course, giving both drivers a fair chance.

Norris may have been keen to get by and attempt to catch Max Verstappen up ahead, but the team felt he had to earn the right to do so.

“I think in this situation, we thought that for Lando to be able to have a chance on Max, he should firstly be able to pass Oscar,” continued Stella. “And the two cars were on the same tyres, same tyre age, same car. So we thought there was no need to interfere with the normal development of the race. We let them race.

“We think that was the right thing to do. I think overall Max was faster, he was just caught in this loop that you have when you lose the slipstream here in Monza, and you have to use the energy to defend from someone else.”

At one late stage Norris flagged a move that he didn’t like, although after the race he acknowledged that Piastri hadn’t done anything wrong. Stella concurred with that view.

“The moment in which Lando put the wheels on the grass, he came on the radio, he made a comment like he pushed me off or something. But actually, when we reviewed it, I think we saw that the episode is much more benign than what it might have looked in the heat of the moment.

Why Gasly ‘is not going to be disappointed’ with P7 from pole

“So I think it's something that certainly we will review, and we will review in the context of this kind of racing. As soon as you fight with each other, then you may lose time. So was there a better way for McLaren to give a fight to Verstappen? We will review. It wasn't obvious to us on the pit wall, and we thought that it was more important to let them race according to our philosophy of going racing.”

A positive aspect of the weekend was that Piastri was back in the fight after some difficult races, and it’s worth remembering that he was P3 in Qualifying before his impeding penalty was applied.

"I think it's a race that confirms a trajectory with Oscar,” said Stella. “We've had a couple of races in which we saw that for the requirements of this year's car, especially in the race when the car slides, we needed to make some adaptations to his natural driving style.

“We kind of adopted the same approach that we used with Lando last year, and we saw pretty rapidly some developments. We were happy to see how competitive Oscar was in Zandvoort in Qualifying trim. We said we need to do a little bit more for the race trim, we put in some work. And it's good that this work seems like it's been useful here in Monza.”

Attention now turns to Madrid and the rest of the season. The obvious question is where might the MCL40 repeat the sort of winning form that it demonstrated at the Hungaroring and the Netherlands?

“I think our tracks will be more the likes of Malaysia, Austin, Brazil,” said Stella. “I think where we have some long corners, the car seems to express its potential well. We have some new upgrades that we will take to Baku, but we still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.

“In Zandvoort and Hungary we were in position to win races, and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race. Drag will be less important in Madrid.

“But from a championship point of view, I think we have to remain very realistic – don't get conditioned by looking at the classification, just focus on one race at a time.”

title: Hamilton calls on Ferrari 'to change things' after Italian GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has called on Ferrari "to change things" in how it manages the intra-team battle between the seven-time World Champion and Charles Leclerc following last weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

The Tifosi had high hopes of a strong result in Sunday's 53-lap race Monza, with Leclerc and Hamilton occupying the second row of the grid.

But the race quickly unravelled as Hamilton dropped to the fringes of the top 10 after finding the gravel on the exit of the first chicane having gone side-by-side with Leclerc, who in turn crashed heavily at the end of the second lap.

Hamilton was eventually able to salvage P6 at the end of the race, but described the result as "devastating" and "a tough one to swallow" having failed to capitalise on a strong starting position.

"Look, I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space, so I don't think they should be worried about me," said Hamilton when asked to give his views on the first corner incident with Leclerc.

"I mean, I've come into the team and tried to be respectful of space and definitely not put the team in jeopardy. I stand by that and that's all I can talk about on my side.

"You have to speak to Fred [Vasseur, Team Principal] about the other side and the decisions that are taken there, but I'll keep pushing and trying to get more from the team and from our car and from the engineers and design and everything like that."

Hamilton's upturn in form during his sophomore season with Ferrari, which includes a maiden Grand Prix victory with the Scuderia in Barcelona and four further podiums, has at times put him in direct competition with Leclerc.

The pair battled fiercely in China, while Hamilton was left angry over the radio in the Netherlands as the Briton was held up by Leclerc while on a different strategy that potentially cost him a chance at a podium.

Hamilton continued to explain that he believes Ferrari need to change their approach in how they go racing, with Mercedes notably managing team orders between its drivers despite both Kimi Antonelli and George Russell fighting for the drivers' title.

"Ultimately, it comes from the top," added Hamilton. "It trickles down the decisions, and so it starts with Fred. There's only so much you can say, so much you can push and shout from the mountain top.

"Yesterday I said that we've got to look at just how we communicate, because if we continue to travel the same path, we get the same result. And it's like, we keep getting the same result.

"We've got to change things, because this is not helping us to move forward. I think they were receptive to it and we'll take it offline...probably not for next week, but particularly after the next race to try and look how we can procedurally do things different so the same thing can't keep happening."

title: Audi lodge 'intention to appeal' over Tsunoda decision
excerpt:
Audi have notified the FIA of their "intention to appeal" after Yuki Tsunoda avoided any penalty for a potential starting infraction at the Italian Grand Prix.

Following Charles Leclerc's crash on the second lap of Sunday's 53-lap race at Monza, the red flag was deployed to repair barrier damage before a standing restart took place.

However, drivers were sent round for a further formation lap after Tsunoda, making his second appearance of the season for Racing Bulls, made a late change of direction into the correct grid box when he realised he was heading for the wrong grid position.

Once the race resumed, Tsunoda eventually finished in 10th to claim the final point on offer, with the Japanese driver not penalised due to several factors, according to the stewards.

"Car 22 approached the grid initially heading for the left hand side of the grid, then realising he was headed for the wrong grid position, the driver changed direction and positioned his car in the correct grid box and in the correct position within the grid box," read the stewards' document on the incident.

"This was verified by the stewards with video from multiple camera angles. The Race Director, in evidence, stated that it was his call, based on the behaviour of the car on the approach to the grid box, to commence an extra formation lap. He stated he was not comfortable starting the race with the car in that position."

The document went on to say that "at no time was the team advised that Race Control considered Car 22 to be the cause of the extra formation lap", and so couldn't advise Tsunoda to start from the pit lane as per Article B5.9.4 of the F1 2026 sporting regulations.

The stewards ultimately concluded that "the extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of Car 22."

Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto finished P11, just missing out on points and prompting the team to inform the FIA of its intention to appeal.

A statement from Audi read: "Following the Italian Grand Prix, we raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there.

"The stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal. As the matter is now subject to the FIA appeal process, we will not comment further at this stage."

title: Could Antonelli have won the Italian GP without the VSC?
excerpt:
Lining up 19th on the grid of his home Italian Grand Prix, Kimi Antonelli must have been cursing the Mercedes algorithms.

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said it was the algorithm that dictated Antonelli take a back-of-grid engine penalty at his home race because the computers “don’t take [drivers’] nationality into consideration”.

Those same systems told him he had no chance of winning the race. A top-five finish was his likely result, and even after making his monumental comeback to lead the race on Lap 18, his tyre strategy should have limited him to second place at best.

title: Bernie Ecclestone arrested for second illegal firearms incident
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 supremo Bernie Ecclestone has described a run-in with Portuguese police as "wall-to-wall aggravation" after he was stopped at a private aerodrome near Lisbon carrying an unlicensed shotgun.

Ecclestone, 95, was reportedly detained at Tires Aerodrome in Cascais, close to Lisbon, after arriving by private jet from Saanen in Switzerland, where he owns a £23 million ski chalet. The former F1 chief had brought the shotgun with him for the purpose of clay-pigeon shooting.

Ecclestone confirmed he had been travelling without the correct documentation for the firearm and was held up for several hours as a result. His wife Fabiana Flosi, 49, subsequently travelled to Lisbon to try to resolve the matter.

"I had a gun that I was bringing over from Switzerland to Portugal for clay-pigeon shooting," Ecclestone told the Daily Mail. "It's as simple as that. I have guns at home there that are licensed."

Ecclestone's wife sorting out the situation

Ecclestone explained that the issue only arose after customs had initially been cleared without incident.

"We cleared customs on arriving here," he said. "I know the guys there, and they were fine with everything. No problems.

"Then a policeman afterwards asked to search the bag. It could have been [his six-year-old son] Ace's fishing tackle for all it looked like, but it wasn't."

When officers enquired about a 'blue book', the documentation required to transport the firearm legally, Ecclestone conceded he was carrying the required paperwork.

"They said they would arrest me, but after what seemed like hours, we sorted it out, but it has been wall-to-wall aggravation," he said.

"But it seems it can be put right. Fabi has gone to Lisbon to surrender the gun, or pay the tax or whatever you need to bring it in."

It is not the first time Ecclestone has found himself in such a situation. In May 2022, he was arrested at an airport in Brazil for illegally carrying a firearm while boarding a private plane, describing that episode as a "silly, tiny little incident" before being released after paying bail

title: Kimi Antonelli makes F1 history as Ferrari falter at Monza - Italian GP winners and losers
excerpt:
An extraordinary Italian Grand Prix delivered and then some, but who stood out, and who floundered?

Monza delivered everything it usually promises: chaos, strategy, heartbreak and a result that nobody quite saw coming.

A red flag, a virtual safety car and a 20-year-old Italian driving the race of his life made the 2026 Italian Grand Prix one of the most memorable in recent memory.

Here are RacingNews365's winners and losers from a dramatic weekend at the Temple of Speed.

Winner - Kimi Antonelli

Starting 19th on the grid after a power unit penalty, the championship leader turned the Italian Grand Prix into his personal coming-of-age moment.

A perfectly executed comeback drive concluded with a late move on Mercedes team-mate George Russell for the lead, becoming the first Italian in 60 years to win on home soil. Only John Watson, in the 1983 United States GP West, has won from lower on the grid - 22nd.

For a 20-year-old Italian to win at Monza, in a championship-leading car, while recovering from the back of the grid to stretch his advantage to 66 points, the title is very much his to lose.

© XPBimages

Winner - Mercedes

A one-two finish at Monza - remarkably, the team's first since the season-opening grand prix in Australia - is about as good as it gets, and Mercedes earned it.

Russell was quick all weekend and led for most of the race, while the team's apparent decision to split strategies under the VSC proved crucial in shaping the result.

The W17 was simply the fastest car around Monza's low-downforce layout. With their lead in the constructors' battle now looking increasingly comfortable, 2026 is shaping up to be a dominant year for the Silver Arrows.

© XPBimages

Winner - Pierre Gasly

Pierre Gasly delivered a maiden pole position with a stunning lap in Q3 that edged out Russell by six hundredths of a second, a result that underlined just how competitive the team's low-drag package was over a single lap.

The result even had Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff thumping his television screen; such was his frustration.

Seventh in the race, though, was always the realistic ceiling once race pace came into play, but just under three seconds behind Lewis Hamilton in a Ferrari is a result that speaks for itself. A genuinely positive weekend for a team that needed one.

© XPBimages

Loser - Charles Leclerc

Of all the places for it to go wrong for Charles Leclerc, it had to be Monza.

Leclerc lost the rear of his SF-26 exiting Parabolica on the second lap, burying the car in the barriers at an estimated 60G in a crash that brought out the red flag.

He walked away unhurt, which is the only positive to take from a nightmare afternoon at his team's home race.

Ferrari had genuine pace, and Leclerc was in the mix before it all unravelled. The championship picture has not moved in his favour.

© XPBimages

Loser - Aston Martin

Zero points from Monza is damaging at the best of times. In the context of 2026, it is another blow for Aston Martin to a season that has consistently promised more than it has delivered.

Fernando Alonso started from the pit lane after power unit changes, ran wide at Turn 7 and sustained damage that ended his race after 23 laps.

Lance Stroll made it a double retirement when a hydraulic failure brought out the VSC around half-distance. Adrian Newey's first full season with the team is not going to plan, and there is still a long way to go.

© XPBimages

Loser - Ferrari

Leclerc's early crash was damaging enough, but the deeper story of Ferrari's Italian Grand Prix was one of a team that does not yet know what it wants to be. The rules of engagement between Lewis Hamilton and Leclerc remain frustratingly unclear, and Monza did little to resolve that.

It is a dynamic that cost the team at Zandvoort, where Hamilton sat behind Leclerc on fresher tyres while Mercedes executed a clean swap between their drivers without hesitation. Ferrari hesitated then, and the uncertainty has not gone away.

Hamilton's sixth-place finish, on worn tyres after Ferrari chose not to act under the VSC, felt like a consequence of the same indecision rather than a considered strategic call.

With two strong drivers who have differing views on the car and contrasting setup preferences, the risk is that Ferrari ends up serving neither particularly well. At their home race, in front of the tifosi, that is a problem they can no longer afford to leave unresolved.

title: Max Verstappen responds to Loek Hartog's life-saving act
excerpt:
The remarkable actions of Loek Hartog over the weekend have not gone unnoticed by Max Verstappen, after Hartog saved the life of fellow racing driver Ollie Millroy.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion took a moment after the Italian Grand Prix at Monza to praise his fellow Dutchman for an act of bravery that captured the attention of the entire motorsport world.

Hartog was competing in the fourth round of the China GT Championship at the Shanghai International Circuit, driving his Porsche 911 GT3 R EVO, when a chain-reaction collision engulfed rival Millroy's Ferrari in flames.

The British driver was trapped in the cockpit as marshals stood hesitantly on the sideline, seemingly unsure how to respond to the burning wreck.

Hartog did not hesitate. He brought his own car to a halt, sprinted towards the fire, grabbed a fire extinguisher from a marshal and physically hauled Millroy to safety. The entire rescue took just 49 seconds.

Following the Italian Grand Prix, in which Verstappen finished third behind Mercedes pair Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, he was asked by Viaplay for his reaction to his compatriot's intervention. The Red Bull driver's admiration was plain to see.

"Yes, that is incredible. He did that really well. A lot of respect for that. Without him, he wouldn't have survived. Yes, very special," said Verstappen.

Millroy sustained five broken ribs, a broken collarbone, a broken hand and a bruised lung, but survived the incident.

From his hospital bed, he said that he owes his life to Hartog. The rescue has been praised globally by media outlets, fellow drivers and fans alike.

title: George Russell strikes defiant tone after 'real tough' spell
excerpt:
George Russell is choosing to look at the bigger picture after Kimi Antonelli denied him victory at the Italian Grand Prix, pointing to a marked improvement in his form since the summer break.

Russell started second on the grid at Monza and led the majority of the race, only to be overhauled by his Mercedes team-mate in the closing laps after the 20-year-old took advantage of a Virtual Safety Car to pit for fresh tyres.

Having started 19th following a power unit penalty, Antonelli's charge through the field was remarkable, and Russell was generous in his assessment of his team-mate's performance.

"It was obviously a great race all around from a neutral perspective," the Briton told media, including RacingNews365. "As soon as I saw Kimi up to P5 after just a handful of laps, I knew he was going to be in the fight with us.

"So clearly that was a very impressive opening few laps, and it was just very challenging to break the slipstream. I think whoever was leading would then be vulnerable to being overtaken again, so I think that's what helped drag a lot of cars along in those early laps."

A welcome change from Russell's pre-summer woes

Although his second-place finish will be a difficult pill to swallow, given where Antonelli started, it continued the trend that has had Russell in far better spirits than before the shutdown.

His run into the summer break was particularly brutal, and ended a painful period in which Russell was looking for answers to his wayward form.

A first-lap collision at Spa-Francorchamps with Lewis Hamilton ended his race on the spot, and a subdued seventh at the Hungaroring meant he scored just six points across the final two rounds before the break.

That came after a strong three-race stretch of podiums, including victory in Austria, but the momentum evaporated over that final double-header before the summer.

Since the season resumed, the picture has been considerably brighter. Russell won the sprint at Zandvoort before finishing third in the Dutch Grand Prix, and followed that with his front-running display at Monza, despite finishing almost four seconds behind Antonelli.

"But I'm going to take the positives from the weekend because, for me personally, pre-summer break it was a real tough run of form," the seven-time grand prix winner added.

"Come back since the break, with the sprint and the two races, we've been in the top three in all of them.

"So, of course, I would have loved to have won today, but the performance is far better than I've had pre-shutdown."

title: 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix - Monza Driver Ratings
excerpt:
Check out RacingNews365's driver ratings from the 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

7 September 2:45PM

It is time for the 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix driver ratings!

The Monza weekend was a wild one, with shocks, surprises and a huge accident for Charles Leclerc in front of the Scuderia.

Did anyone get a perfect 10? And who finds themselves at the bottom of RacingNews365's Monza rankings? Find out below!

The top five

Kimi Antonelli - 10

What a way to end a 60-year wait. Antonelli qualified seventh but was dropped to 19th on the grid after Mercedes took an engine penalty at his home race, a bold strategic gamble that paid off in spectacular fashion. From the back of the field, the 20-year-old carved his way through with 26 overtakes, pitting under the Virtual Safety Car for fresh medium tyres and then reeling in team-mate George Russell, whose hard tyres were fading badly. The decisive move came at Ascari on lap 50 of 53, and Antonelli swept to victory with the fastest lap to boot. The first Italian to win at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966, and a performance that will live long in the memory.

Pierre Gasly - 9.5

Saturday belonged to Gasly. His maiden Formula 1 pole position, 191 grands prix into his career, was Alpine's first since Fernando Alonso put Renault on pole at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix. The Frenchman delivered a stunning 1:21.786 in Q3 to pip Russell by six hundredths of a second, a lap that was no fluke given Alpine's pace throughout qualifying. The race told a different story, as it so often does for a midfield car at the sharp end. Gasly held the lead off the line but was gradually swallowed by faster machinery as the laps wore on, ultimately finishing seventh, some 27 seconds behind Antonelli. A brilliant Saturday, a sobering Sunday, but the pole alone elevates this weekend significantly.

Max Verstappen - 8.5

Verstappen qualified sixth, promoted to fifth on the grid after Oscar Piastri's penalty for impeding Liam Lawson, and produced a typically combative drive to finish on the podium. He briefly led the race around lap 12, using overtake mode to dive past Russell into the first chicane, though Mercedes' superior race pace soon reasserted itself. A rear-axle issue complicated his afternoon, but Verstappen pitted under the Virtual Safety Car and used fresh rubber to battle his way past Gasly, Norris and Hamilton. A lock-up at Turn 1 briefly let Piastri through, but the Dutchman repassed around lap 43 and held third to the flag, 14.7 seconds behind Antonelli. Extracting a podium from the RB22 at Monza was no small feat.

George Russell - 8

Russell was arguably the fastest driver all weekend, topping both FP2 and FP3 before qualifying on the front row, just 0.060 seconds behind Gasly. He took the lead on lap two and controlled proceedings for the majority of the 53-lap distance, managing pressure from Verstappen and, increasingly, from Antonelli behind. The critical moment came under the Virtual Safety Car. Mercedes pitted Antonelli for fresh mediums while Russell stayed out on worn hard tyres, a strategy call that ultimately doomed him. By the closing laps his rubber was spent, and Antonelli swept past on lap 50. Second place and 18 points represents a strong haul, but Russell will know a victory slipped through his fingers through no real fault of his own.

Franco Colapinto - 8

Colapinto put in a superb qualifying session, reaching Q3 and setting the eighth-fastest time to line up seventh on the grid after Antonelli's penalty. On the restart following Charles Leclerc's heavy Parabolica crash, the Argentine was right in the mix, scrapping with Verstappen for third place. Then came the mistake. An off-track moment on lap six sent him tumbling from fourth to 16th, and what could have been a career-best result suddenly looked like a disaster. To his credit, Colapinto regrouped and mounted a determined recovery, picking his way back through the field to finish ninth and score two points for Alpine. The error will sting, but the raw pace and the fightback deserve recognition.

© XPBimages

The bottom five

Valtteri Bottas - 5

A Q1 exit left Bottas 19th in qualifying, though grid penalties for others promoted him to a P16 start on race day. It was a small mercy for the Cadillac driver, who could do little with it. On a circuit where straight-line speed is king, the Cadillac simply lacked the grunt to compete, and Bottas slipped backwards throughout the afternoon. He was eventually classified 19th, two laps down on the leaders, and last of the runners still circulating. It was a weekend to forget for the Finn, with very little to take away from Monza.

Charles Leclerc - 4.5

Leclerc qualified a respectable fourth for Ferrari's home race and looked well placed to deliver a solid result. Instead, disaster struck on lap two. Fighting to defend his position from Oscar Piastri at the exit of Parabolica, Leclerc lost the rear of the SF-26, snapped sideways and hit the tyre barrier at enormous speed in what was reported as a roughly 60G impact. The crash triggered a red flag, and while Leclerc walked away and was cleared by the FIA medical centre, his race was over before it had truly begun. A bitterly disappointing home weekend for the Monégasque.

Liam Lawson - 4

Lawson's qualifying pace was respectable in isolation, with the New Zealander reaching Q2 and clocking a 1:22.821 to finish 14th in the session. However, a 35-place power unit penalty condemned him to a pit-lane start. He made impressive early progress through the field, but contact with Nico Hulkenberg at the red-flag restart damaged his front wing and cost him over 30 seconds in an unscheduled pit stop. That incident effectively ended his chances of scoring points, and he finished 14th, roughly 17 seconds adrift of the final points-paying position.

Fernando Alonso - 3.5

Both Aston Martins endured a wretched weekend at Monza. Alonso was eliminated in Q1 with a 1:25.150, good enough only for 21st on the grid, before his race came to a premature end following a suspension failure. Reports indicate the Spaniard struck the kerbs aggressively, which caused damage to the underside of the car and ultimately broke the front-right suspension, forcing him to pit on lap 23 and retire. At 45, Alonso has seen better weekends, and this was one he will want to move past quickly.

Lance Stroll - 3.5

Stroll fared no better than his team-mate, qualifying last of the 22 drivers in P22 with a 1:25.222 after being knocked out in Q1. His race was then cut short by a hydraulic failure that brought his AMR26 to a halt near the first chicane. With both cars failing to see the chequered flag, Monza was a deeply frustrating outing for Aston Martin. For Stroll, there was simply nothing to salvage from a weekend where the car let him down both on pace and reliability.

title: McLaren confirm review after Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri almost come to blows
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has said the team will review Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri's late-race battle at the Italian Grand Prix, particularly given it may have cost them the chance to fight Max Verstappen for the final podium position.

The two drivers engaged in some spirited on-track action in the final few laps at Monza, with the former ultimately outlasting the latter for fourth place.

However, it could have ended in tears, with the pair almost colliding on Lap 51 of 53, when Norris tried to overtake around the outside of the Curva Grande, the fast, sweeping right-hander that leads into the second chicane at the Temple of Speed.

Defending his position, Piastri moved over to the left, blocking his team-mate, who had to take to the grass.

The reigning F1 drivers' champion was less than impressed, taking to team radio to express his displeasure, saying the Australian had pushed him off.

Norris subsequently revised his account after the race, taking a much more measured view of the incident.

When asked about the episode, the McLaren boss detailed why the team did not intervene, despite the British driver appearing to have more pace in hand.

"In this situation, we thought that for Lando to be able to have a chance on Max, he should first be able to pass Oscar," Stella explained to media, including RacingNews365.

"And the two cars were on the same tyres, the same tyre age, the same car. So we thought there was no need to interfere with the normal development of the race. We let them race.

"We think that was the right thing to do. I think overall Max was faster. He was just caught in this hook that you have this year, when you lose the slipstream here in Monza, and you have to use the energy to defend from someone else."

Was there a 'better way' to fight Verstappen?

Addressing the near miss between his two drivers, Stella, like Norris and Piastri in their post-race press duties, dismissed any wrongdoing.

"The moment in which Lando put the wheels on the grass, he came on the radio; he made a comment like 'he pushed me off' or something," the Italian added.

"But actually, when we reviewed it, I think we saw that the episode is much more benign than what it might have looked like in the heat of the moment."

Nonetheless, the 55-year-old did state that McLaren would look more closely at the scenario, in large part due to the lost opportunity to attack the Red Bull ahead, which took the chequered flag five seconds ahead of Norris.

"So it's something that we will certainly review, and we will review it in the context of this kind of racing, because I think you are right in highlighting that as soon as you fight with each other, then you may lose time," Stella said.

"So, was there a better way for McLaren to give a fight to Verstappen? We will review.

"It wasn't obvious to us on the pit wall, and we thought that it was more important to let them race according to our philosophy of going racing."

title: Fred Vasseur hints at potential Ferrari team orders change
excerpt:
Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur has indicated a willingness to now consider invoking team orders, even though Lewis Hamilton feels doing so would be too little, too late.

Fred Vasseur has suggested he will discuss team orders with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc after the Italian Grand Prix.

Until now, the Ferrari team principal has been reticent to implement them and was quick to highlight how McLaren would have handed Max Verstappen the F1 drivers' championship last season if the Woking-based squad had backed Oscar Piastri at this stage of the campaign.

However, with Hamilton's advantage over Leclerc growing to 36 points after the Monegasque driver crashed out at Monza, Vasseur has indicated a willingness to consider them.

The subject came acutely back into focus at the Temple of Speed, when the two drivers clashed through the opening chicane on the first lap, which cost Hamilton dearly.

The seven-time F1 drivers' champion had got up the inside of his team-mate into Turn 1, which put him on the outside for Turn 2, with Leclerc — intended or otherwise — shuffling him out wide onto the gravel.

Hamilton dropped to tenth, costing the Scuderia any opportunity to work together strategically. Not that it would matter, with Leclerc crashing heavily at the Curva Alboreto (the Parabolica) the following lap.

Vasseur, however, did not want to talk about the first lap incident until he had been given the chance to address it with his drivers.

"I spoke with Lewis for two seconds, and not at all with Charles, so we have had no time to discuss it," he responded to media, including RacingNews365, when asked if he had spoken to his drivers about the incident on the first lap.

When the follow-up pressed him on whether he had any thoughts on what happened, Vasseur replied: "No, I prefer to discuss with them first rather than with you first."

McLaren and Max Verstappen comparison

Hamilton has been calling for Ferrari to start prioritising him in his bid for a record-breaking eighth F1 drivers' championship, but he slumped to 76 points adrift of Kimi Antonelli after his sixth-place finish at Monza.

The 41-year-old called out the Italian team in his post-race media duties, lamenting the lack of rules of engagement, something he believes must be addressed, particularly after his clash with Leclerc.

And as for the possibility of the Prancing Horse throwing its weight behind him, Hamilton added: "It's far too late for those decisions to come. It's many, many weeks too late."

Vasseur, on the other hand, sees the situation differently, and feels that only now is it the time to consider enacting team orders.

"For sure, the outcome of [Turns] 1 and 2 is not good for the team, if that's the question," the Frenchman said, opening up about the first lap.

"Now, to see if we have a team order or whatever, I think that the good comparison that I made was that last year Piastri was leading McLean at this stage of the season, and if McLaren put everything on Piastri, Max Verstappen would have been champion."

"But for sure, at one stage you have to make a decision. But I think it was too early to make a decision before Monza. Now we have time to discuss with the guys."

title: Red Bull set 'ultimate speed' target after Max Verstappen heroics
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has set the Austrian marque the target of finding "that ultimate speed", something he feels it is lacking despite Max Verstappen's heroic Monza podium.

The Dutchman started the Italian Grand Prix from fifth and quickly worked his way towards the front, overtaking Charles Leclerc and Pierre Gasly in rapid fashion.

Verstappen's early-race pace was impressive, with the four-time world champion even briefly taking the lead after passing George Russell.

However, the 28-year-old quickly fell back behind Russell and then Kimi Antonelli, who charged through the field to win from 19th on the grid.

A mid-race pit stop for fresh tyres dropped Verstappen to seventh, although he worked his way back through the field to claim an impressive third-place podium finish.

It was the best on offer for the Red Bull star, with Mercedes simply having a pace advantage that he could not compete with throughout the race.

Mekies was in awe of what Verstappen achieved and hopes that finding better car speed will improve the team's overall performance.

"It was a well-deserved podium for Max and the whole team," said Mekies. "It was an intense weekend, but the race showed that our pace was fairly strong.

"Mercedes was a bit too fast for us but we were strong enough to beat Ferrari and McLaren on merits. It was probably our best race pace in a few weeks and a step in the right direction.

"We won't be happy until we have that ultimate speed and we clearly still have some challenges to overcome, which may unlock more performance once we get to the bottom of them.

"Max has been incredible on track. He made several very spectacular overtakes and defensive manoeuvres and drove an aggressive strategy which led us to the podium."

title: Kimi Antonelli opens up on victory-chance belief after stunning recovery
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has opened up on whether he believed victory was possible in the Italian Grand Prix after his stunning recovery to win from 19th on home soil.

The championship leader started from the penultimate row of the grid following a power unit change, with the components having been outside of his legal pool.

Going into the race, the Italian had hopes of a podium, although his eyes quickly turned to a potential race win after climbing to 12th before a red flag on the third lap.

From the race restart, Antonelli made rapid progress towards the front, where he exchanged positions with George Russell on several occasions.

Antonelli ultimately dropped to sixth after pitting during a short Virtual Safety Car period, but, on fresher tyres, he breezed to the front to claim a famous win.

Asked what he thought was possible on the grid, Antonelli said: "I thought a podium was possible, but then obviously with the red flag I was already P12, and then I knew that I could have had a shot to it.

"But, of course, you know, then I found myself at the front and battling, but it was very difficult to break away, basically impossible. So I knew it would have been difficult.

"Then with the VSC we pitted and then we had to close the gap and, yeah, then in the end to bring it home, very happy with that."

Monza boasts arguably the most incredible podium celebrations of the season, which were further heightened by the fact that Antonelli was the first Italian winner of the Italian GP since 1966.

It was an emotional occasion for the youngster, who now leads the drivers' championship by 66 points over Russell.

Discussing the reaction from the fans while on the podium, Antonelli added: Yeah, I think this is the most special podium of the season.

"To see all the fans on the straight, it’s just incredible. And then, of course, you know, being at home, it adds that little bit of extra. And, yeah, super, super happy with that."

title: Charles Leclerc hits back at anti-teamwork Lewis Hamilton 'narrative'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has hit back at a "narrative" that he and Lewis Hamilton are not working together following a disastrous Italian Grand Prix.

Discussions about the Ferrari pair not working together were brought up in Zandvoort before it all went horribly wrong at the first two corners in Monza.

Both Scuderia drivers started on the second row, with Hamilton opting for an aggressive move down the inside of Leclerc at the first corner.

This forced Leclerc to take a different line into Turn 2, which resulted in his seven-time world champion teammate being left with nowhere to go but the gravel on the exit of the corner.

Hamilton tumbled from fourth to 10th and immediately complained over the radio, only for Leclerc to crash out of the race at the end of the second lap and trigger a red flag.

Leclerc lost control of his SF-26 on the exit of Parabolica, resulting in barrier repairs being needed while his destroyed car also required retrieval.

However, what happened at the first corners came up after the race in the media pen, with Leclerc insisting that the talk of the duo not working together was false.

Asked about the narrative of himself and Hamilton not working together, the Monegasque told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah, I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other.

"I mean, honestly, Zandvoort, there were way too many talks already. Here, it's true, though, that we went too far.

"I think Lewis in Turn 1, then Turn 2, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough. And doing it here is not good."

title: Franco Colapinto breaks down in tears after 'wasted' opportunity
excerpt:
A crestfallen Franco Colapinto could not conceal his emotions after an error at the restart of the Italian Grand Prix saw him tumble down the order from third on the road.

The Alpine driver, who started seventh at Monza, cleverly capitalised on the Charles Leclerc-induced red flag to get himself into fourth, dumping his remaining battery and passing Oscar Piastri before the race was stopped.

At the resumption, the Argentine driver briefly overtook Max Verstappen for third, behind team-mate Pierre Gasly, but made a costly mistake at the first Lesmo corner.

Running fourth at the time, Colapinto ran wide onto the gravel, falling to P15 as any chance of the Alpines working together fell by the wayside.

Speaking on TV after the 53-lap contest, the 23-year-old was distraught and could not hold back his tears, having thrown away a crucial chance.

"It could have been... a great race and a... major mistake," the Alpine driver told ESPN and DAZN cameras in Spanish after the race.

"So... I wasted a very important opportunity for the team and for myself."

Nonetheless, Colapinto put together an impressive recovery drive, getting his A526 back up to ninth by the chequered flag, just two places behind Gasly in seventh, but he seemingly could not escape the feeling it could have been so much more.

He added: "So, a bit sad, but... I need to learn from this and keep pushing."

title: Max Verstappen hails Red Bull response after pointed criticism
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has commended Red Bull for the recovery the Milton Keynes-based outfit engineered with his RB22 across the Italian Grand Prix weekend, describing it as a "strong turnaround" after a bruising period for the team.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion finished on the podium at Monza, a result that seemed improbable just 48 hours earlier when he cut a frustrated figure during Friday practice, complaining of balance issues and a lack of pace after missing FP1 entirely due to Ayumu Iwasa's mandatory rookie running and ending FP2 only ninth fastest.

The round at the Temple of Speed came off the back of Red Bull's recent nadir at Zandvoort, where the Dutchman qualified a lowly seventh and crashed out on the opening lap in damp conditions.

He was blunt in his assessment there, saying the RB22 was "not really to my liking" and that Red Bull lacked the pace to fight at the front.

His criticism sharpened further in the build-up to Monza, where he warned the weekend would be "really painful" given the energy deployment limitations of his car — amid the controversial new power unit regulations — at such a power-hungry circuit. The pessimism appeared justified on Friday.

Yet Red Bull found something overnight, as the team so often does, given it has become somewhat of a calling card. Verstappen qualified sixth, benefited from Oscar Piastri's grid penalty, and went on to secure a podium finish in third behind the dominant Mercedes pair of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

Masked problems

Even so, Verstappen made clear the result masked significant struggles during the race itself, particularly against Mercedes-powered machinery on Monza's long straights.

"I had my issues in qualifying that, of course, were still there," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365. "But also, I think it was quite clear during the race that we just can't keep up with the deployment of the Mercedes-powered cars, and that is, of course, on a track like Monza, very tough.

"Of course, with the overtake mode it looked quite promising, but as soon as I got in the lead, it was very hard to defend, and that has been a bit my problem throughout the whole race.

"Even when we had the VSC, we boxed, had better tyres, I'm overtaking cars, but as soon as they, you know, can hang in that overtake mode, it's just too powerful for us to actually really defend that, even on better tyres. So, it took me a while even to clear the McLarens."

Despite those frustrations, Verstappen acknowledged the broader significance of the result given how far Red Bull had fallen at Zandvoort, where his first-lap retirement and the team's lack of competitiveness prompted pointed criticism of the car's direction.

"But for us to be on the podium, I think after a very difficult weekend in Zandvoort, where the car was not really to my liking, yeah, we managed to have a strong turnaround from Friday to Saturday, and the car was definitely in a better window," he added.

"But we still have a few bits and areas that we know need to be better, plus the obvious deployment on the straights."

title: Lewis Hamilton concedes to crucial Ferrari setback: 'Far too late'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes it is “far too late” for Ferrari to start increasing its teamwork in pursuit of the 2026 title.

Hamilton came to blows with Charles Leclerc on the opening lap, feeling he was pushed wide on the exit of Turn 2 by his team-mate.

The seven-time champion ran through the gravel and emerged down the order, forcing him into a recovery drive for the rest of the race.

Ferrari lost further ground to Mercedes after the Silver Arrows ended the race with maximum points, while Hamilton crossed the line in sixth place.

With Hamilton being closer to Mercedes in the standings than Leclerc for some time, some suggested at recent events that Ferrari should throw its support behind the former in order to maximise its chance of success this year.

But with Kimi Antonelli stretching out his lead following another win, Hamilton asserted it is too late for such decisions.

“We just lost so much ground on points [on Sunday],” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“It’s far too late for those decisions to come. It’s many, many weeks too late.

“All I can do is turn up. I’ll get up tomorrow morning and give my best.”

Ferrari's day went from bad to worse as Leclerc's race ended shortly after his skirmish with Hamilton, when he lost control of his car and crashed at the final corner.

While Hamilton did not completely rule out his chances of a title this year, he conceded the 76-point gap to Antonelli will likely be very difficult to overcome.

“Ultimately, I feel massively gutted for the Tifosi, who showed up for us today,” he said.

“The guys back at the factory, who really are giving it everything. [On Saturday] we didn’t really execute that well, and the same today.

“It’s tough because I’m giving it everything I can, but sometimes it’s not enough. You need all the other stuff to come together.

“It’s never over until it’s over.

“[But] it’s an amount that, with the pace that they have, it’s a very difficult amount to close up.”
